headline: The Runestone, the Historian, and the Quote He Probably Never Wrote
lede: Buried in a Twitter thread about a disputed Minnesota rune stone are two incendiary quotes attributed to Sven Lagerbring, an eighteenth-century Swedish scholar, claiming that Odin was a Turk and that Germanic civilization descends from Turkic forebears. Lagerbring was a real and significant historian who did once publish a fringe essay on Swedish-Turkish linguistic kinship. The specific words in the image are almost certainly invented.
body:
The image in this thread sets a recognizable trap. Anchored to a discussion of the **Kensington Runestone** — a disputed carved stone found in Minnesota in 1898 that claims to record a fourteenth-century Norse expedition — it presents two incendiary quotes attributed to Sven Lagerbring, described as “the Father of Swedish Historiography.” The quotes assert that Odin was a Turk, that Germanic peoples are of Turkic origin, and that anyone saying otherwise is trying to deceive you. The framing is calibrated to produce the sensation of suppressed truth.

Lagerbring was a genuine and significant scholar. Born in 1707, he spent his career at Lund University, where his four-volume *Swea rikes historia* (1769–1783) applied source criticism to Swedish medieval records in ways that were genuinely innovative for the era. He did, early in his career, write a 1764 fringe essay — *Bref om Svenska och Turkiska Språkens likhet* (“Letter on the Similarities of Swedish and Turkish Languages”) — proposing that Swedes had Turkic ancestors, based on superficial word-parallels and on passages in Norse sagas describing Odin as having migrated from a land called “Tyrkland.” That hypothesis was considered eccentric even in the eighteenth century and was rejected by subsequent scholars; Wikipedia’s own article on Lagerbring calls it “pseudoscientific.”

The specific quotes in the image are a different matter. The dramatic first-person register (“I don’t care whether it will be discrediting for me or not”), the misspellings of “Geto” and “Tracian,” and the complete absence of any citation — no page number, no original Swedish text, no scholarly translation — are all red flags. These quotes circulate exclusively on Turkish nationalist social media, YouTube channels, and meme accounts; no academic edition or translation of Lagerbring’s work reproduces them. The underlying textual authority the whole argument rests on — Snorri Sturluson’s *Prose Edda* (c. 1220), which describes Odin migrating from a city near the Black Sea called “Tyrkland” — is a medieval literary device called *euhemerism*: the practice of recasting pagan gods as historical human rulers, used by Christian scholars who wanted to engage with pre-Christian tradition without endorsing polytheism.

The **Kensington Runestone**, meanwhile, is the textbook example of a nineteenth-century hoax. When Scandinavian linguists and *runologists* examined it after its 1898 discovery, they found language resembling modern Swedish rather than any attested fourteenth-century dialect, Arabic-style numerals unique among medieval runestones, and a scrambled *Futhark* — the collective name for Germanic runic writing systems — that mixed Elder and Younger runic traditions in combinations unknown from any verified medieval inscription. Forensic geologist Scott Wolter has argued the stone’s weathering suggests genuine age, but the preponderance of expert opinion holds that it was most likely fabricated by the Swedish immigrant who found it.

The pattern connecting these two items is not accidental. Both the Lagerbring image and the Kensington Runestone serve as props in a broader narrative of hidden or suppressed civilizational history — one that resonates with the **Turkish History Thesis**, a state-sponsored pseudohistorical framework launched at Turkey’s First Historical Congress in 1932. That thesis claimed Turkic peoples spread civilization from Central Asia across the ancient world; its companion, the *Sun Language Theory*, held that all human languages descended from a proto-Turkic original. Both were abandoned after Atatürk’s death in 1938, but the impulse toward Turkic civilizational primacy has persisted in nationalist internet culture, producing exactly this kind of document: a real historian’s name, some almost certainly invented quotes, a genuine medieval text stripped of context, and an American rune stone that most experts regard as a forgery.

concepts.definition: A slab of greywacke found in Douglas County, Minnesota in 1898, bearing a runic inscription that purports to record a 1362 Scandinavian expedition deep into North America. Mainstream linguists and runologists regard it as a nineteenth-century forgery: its language resembles modern Swedish rather than any attested medieval dialect, and its runic forms are inconsistent with any verified medieval inscription.

A literary and intellectual technique, named after the fourth-century BCE Greek philosopher Euhemerus, of explaining mythological figures as deified historical humans. Medieval Christian scholars applied it to pagan gods to engage with pre-Christian tradition without endorsing polytheism. Snorri Sturluson used it when he described Odin as a historical king who migrated from eastern lands — a rhetorical device, not a genealogical claim.

The collective name for the runic writing systems used by Germanic peoples from roughly the second to the twelfth centuries CE, named as an acronym of its first six sounds. The Elder Futhark (24 runes) is the oldest form; the Younger Futhark (16 runes) is what Viking Age runestones typically use. The Kensington stone’s irregular mix of both traditions is one of the core reasons experts identify it as a modern forgery.

A state-sponsored pseudohistorical framework promoted by the Kemalist government at Turkey’s First Historical Congress in 1932, claiming that Turkic peoples originating in Central Asia spread civilization to China, India, the Balkans, and beyond. Its companion was the Sun Language Theory, which held that all human languages descended from a proto-Turkic original. Both were officially abandoned after Atatürk’s death in 1938 but created a lasting template for nationalist claims of Turkic civilizational primacy.

A pseudolinguistic hypothesis promoted by the Turkish state in 1935–1936, claiming all human languages descended from a proto-Turkic primal language. Atatürk personally backed it; it was quietly abandoned after his death in 1938 and is now regarded as an example of state-sponsored linguistic nationalism with no scientific basis.

A scholar who specializes in runic inscriptions — their linguistic content, historical dating, regional forms, and archaeological context. Runologists have been the primary academic voice in debunking the Kensington Runestone, citing linguistic anachronisms and irregular rune forms that no genuine medieval inscription shares.

books.title: Prose Edda
books.author: Snorri Sturluson
books.summary: A thirteenth-century Icelandic compendium of Norse mythology and poetic tradition, composed around 1220 by the Christian scholar and politician Snorri Sturluson. Its prologue recasts the Norse gods as historical human rulers who migrated from a region near the Black Sea that Snorri calls “Tyrkland.” This is the primary text cited by pan-Turkic theorists as evidence that Odin was of Turkic origin, though scholars recognize it as an application of euhemerism rather than historical memory. It is otherwise the single most important secondary source for Norse mythology.

books.title: Swea rikes historia
books.author: Sven Lagerbring
books.summary: A four-volume history of Sweden published between 1769 and 1783, and Lagerbring’s principal scholarly achievement. It applied rigorous source criticism to Swedish medieval records — scrutinizing document authenticity and distinguishing primary from secondary sources — in ways that were genuinely innovative for the eighteenth century. This serious work is categorically distinct from Lagerbring’s earlier 1764 fringe letter proposing Swedish-Turkish linguistic kinship, and it is the basis for his legitimate reputation as a founding figure of modern Swedish historiography.

fact_check: The two quotes attributed to Lagerbring — beginning “Our ancestors are Turks who are comrades of Oden” and “We Germanic People are in Origin Türks” — are almost certainly fabricated or heavily distorted paraphrases. They circulate exclusively on Turkish nationalist social media and meme accounts, never in any academic edition, scholarly translation, or citation-bearing publication. No original Swedish text or verifiable page reference accompanies them. Lagerbring did write a 1764 essay proposing Swedish-Turkish linguistic kinship, but Wikipedia’s own article calls that work “pseudoscientific,” and the specific dramatic language in the image has no traceable scholarly provenance. The Snorri claim that underwrites the broader argument — that Odin’s homeland “Tyrkland” proves Turkic origin — misrepresents a recognized medieval euhemeristic literary device as historical genealogy. The Kensington Runestone, anchor of the parent tweet, is likewise considered a forgery by the preponderance of expert opinion.
